title: NC Early Voting: Church continues Souls to Polls, Social Justice Sunday tradition of marching to polling sites in Durham - ABC11 News
text:
NC Early Voting: Church continues Souls to Polls, Social Justice Sunday tradition of marching to polling sites in Durham - ABC11 Raleigh-Durham 
 24/7 Live Raleigh Durham Fayetteville Surrounding Area SOCIETY 
 St. Joseph AME continues 'Social Justice Sunday' tradition with early voting march in Durham 
 By Bianca Holman Sunday, October 25, 2026 6:10PM 
 Watch Eyewitness News, First Alert Weather, and original programming. DURHAM, N.C. (WTVD) -- Members of St. Joseph AME Church and the surrounding community made their way to the polls Sunday as part of the church's longstanding "Social Justice Sunday" tradition.
 The group gathered at the Durham church before walking and riding to an early voting location.
 "So here we have a motto of love the people, love God, love people who do the work, meaning, you know, try to make the community a better place for all of us concerned," said Jacque Beatty-Smith and Richard Smith of the church's Social Action Committee.
 The Rev. Dr. Abdue Knox, pastor of St. Joseph AME Church, said the event brings together members of the congregation, community and neighboring churches.
 "We have a huge caravan of people from our church, from our community, from neighboring churches where we worship together," Knox said. "And then we all walk and ride over to North Carolina Central to cast their votes."
 Organizers said their efforts also focus on helping people prepare before arriving at the polls, including making sure voters have the information and identification they need.
 "We're looking at ways that we can deal with voter suppression and anything else that voters run into, making sure that they have the basics, their IDs and other information that they need when they go to the polling, being prepared and having a plan," Beatty-Smith and Smith said.

 Knox said encouraging members of the church to participate in elections is part of its broader commitment to community involvement.
 "We maintain that, and the wisdom in the way we do that is encouraging our people to vote and be involved in our community," Knox said.
 Kent Roberson, a guest speaker at the event, also encouraged attendees to recognize their ability to make their voices heard. "We want individuals to know that they do have the power," Roberson said.
 For Knox, participating in the election also carries a connection to previous generations.
 "Let our voices be heard, and that we have the responsibility from our ancestors and for those that are with us now to go vote," Knox said.
